core.text: Put the *-ba-* of the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense) together with the passive endings and you have **the imperfect passive (the 'was being done' form)**: *amā-bā-tur* — she was being loved, she was loved; *nōminā-bā-tur* — he was called; *ego amā-ba-r* — I was loved. The set is *-bar, -bāris, -bātur, -bāmur, -bāminī, -bantur*; the 3rd and 4th conjugations take *-ēbar, -ēbātur* (*mittēbantur* — they were being sent). A deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) uses exactly these forms: *sequēbātur* — he was following. Latin name: imperfectum indicātīvī passīvī.
*Was being praised* is the English passive of the ongoing past: the subject was on the receiving end while it went on.
Stem (+ ē) + ba + -r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur; a deponent has the same shape with an active sense.

invented.en: The boy was being praised by the teacher.

core.text: *amābat* and *amābātur* share the *-ba-*; the *r* decides who does what. *Iūlius uxōrem amābat*, and in the same breath *ab eā amābātur* — he loved her (active) and was loved by her (passive). Person for person: *-bam / -bar*, *-bās / -bāris*, *-bat / -bātur*, *-bāmus / -bāmur*, *-bātis / -bāminī*, *-bant / -bantur*.

more.text: The doer is *ā / ab* + ablative (*ab eā amābātur*); a thing used is a bare ablative (*flūctibus iactābātur* — was tossed by the waves). *vidēbātur* usually means *seemed*, not *was seen*: *sibi fēlīx esse vidēbātur* — he seemed to himself to be happy.

The learner's notes (week 19): the passive and deponent imperfect use the same marker *(e)ba* as the active, with the passive / deponent endings added; the variable vowels drop after the *a*; the first person singular always takes *-r*, never *-or*: *pōnēbar, pulsābar, vidēbar, fugiēbar, audiēbar; pōnēbāris, pōnēbātur, pōnēbāmur, pōnēbāminī, pōnēbantur*.

Ørberg (chapter XIX): *laudābar, laudābāris, laudābātur, laudābāmur, laudābāminī, laudābantur*; *timēbar*; *reprehendēbar, reprehendēbātur*; *pūniēbar*; and in the story *Iūlius uxōrem suam amābat*, then *ab eā amābātur*. A&G §184 give the same table under the first conjugation.
The active and the passive imperfect differ only in their last syllable (*audiēbat* against *audiēbātur*), so read to the end of the word before deciding who is doing what.

teach.title: What the form does

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence says what was being done to the subject?

teach.say: When something was being done *to* the subject, Latin uses the imperfect passive (the 'was being done' form). It keeps the active's *-bā-* and changes only the endings after it; the doer, if named, stands behind *ā* or *ab*. *Puerī ā magistrō vocābantur* — the boys were being called by the teacher.

check.ask: Tap the verb that says the table was having something done to it.

teach.title: The third person: -bātur and -bantur
teach.say: Take the active imperfect and swap its ending for the passive one: *-bat* becomes *-bātur*, *-bant* becomes *-bantur*. That one syllable turns the subject from the doer into the one it is done to: *audiēbat*, he was listening, against *audiēbātur*, he was being heard.

show.say: vocābātur, vocābantur — the active ending with -ur behind it

check.ask: Now the same two cells on laudō: the imperfect passive for 'he, she, it' and for 'they'.

teach.title: The other four persons
teach.say: The rest of the column puts its own passive endings on the same *-bā-*: *-bar* (I), *-bāris* (you), *-bāmur* (we), *-bāminī* (you all). Four of the six end in *-r* or *-ur* — *-bar*, *-bātur*, *-bāmur*, *-bantur* — and two do not: *-bāris* (you) and *-bāminī* (you all). Those two are the ones to remember.

check.ask: Write the imperfect passive of amō for I, for you, for we and for you all.

teach.title: The 3rd and 4th conjugations put -ē- first
teach.say: Exactly as in the active, verbs of the third and fourth conjugations (the conjugation is which of the four families a Latin verb belongs to) slip in an *-ē-* before the marker: *mittēbātur* it was being sent, *aperiēbātur* it was being opened, *carpēbantur* they were being picked. Read the word as stem + ē + bā + passive ending.

show.say: mittēbātur, mittēbantur — the joining -ē- in front of the marker

check.ask: Now the same two cells on dīcō: the imperfect passive for 'he, she, it' and for 'they'.

teach.title: Deponent verbs wear these endings and mean something active
teach.say: Some verbs carry passive endings but have an active meaning: a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks). *Sequēbātur* is not 'he was being followed' but 'he was following'; *loquēbātur* is 'he was talking'. The ending still tells you the tense and the person; the verb itself tells you the meaning.

check.ask: ōsculābātur — who is doing the kissing, Aemilia or her daughter?

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Now build one from the inside out: stem, then *-ē-* if the verb needs it, then *-bā-*, then the passive ending. In the sentence in front of you the roses are the subject, Julia is the doer behind *ā*, and the verb carries both the past and the passive at once.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the imperfect passive of dūcō, third person plural.
